transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
The winner of the Nobel Prize in Economics was just announced.
The Royal Swedish Academy in Stockholm says this year's recipients are Robert Hall of
Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University.
They're being awarded the prize for their research on microeconomics foundation for
macroeconomic stabilization.
President Trump says Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an energy ceasefire, but NPR's
Joanna Kekissos reports Ukraine's account differs from the president's.
Zelensky said on Sunday that he did not know anything about the ceasefire.
This would involve both sides halting attacks on energy facilities.
And in his evening video address Sunday night, Zelensky said he welcomes such a ceasefire.
He's saying let's make it happen.
Ukraine supports real paths to ending this war and is ready to stop striking Russian
energy infrastructure if Russia reciprocates in Ukraine.
NPR's Joanna Kekissos reporting North Korea has conducted what appears to be its fourth
missile launch in the past month, NPR's Anthony Kuhn reports from Seoul.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said the North launched multiple ballistic missiles
which traveled about 560 miles from the Pyongyang area eastward into the sea.
Japan's Defense Ministry says it also detected the launch and warned ships to watch out for
a falling debris.
South Korea's presidential office, known as the Blue House, held an emergency meeting
to discuss the launches, which are called illegal and urge the North to halt.
This month, both North and South Korea have tested hypersonic missiles, which are harder
to track and intercept.
Last week marked the South's first hypersonic test overseen by President Lee Jae-myung, while
the North has conducted several such tests since 2021.
Anthony Kuhn in PR News, Seoul.
Waves are pounding the shore in Long Beach, California in the wake of Tropical Storm Rachel.
Steve Futterman reports damage assessments are underway.
Coastal areas suffered most of the damage.
High tides and powerful waves battered beach cities, including Long Beach, Newport Beach,
and in the San Diego area, Imperial Beach.
Some oceanfront homes were hit very hard.
The boardwalk in Long Beach suffered significant damage.
Many streets were flooded.
In some cases, drivers had to be rescued from their cars.
There were similar reports of damage to the South in Baja, California.
This could be a preview of things to come, as forecasters predict a very strong El Nino
weather pattern during the upcoming months, which will bring additional powerful storms.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman in Los Angeles.
This is NPR News.
Prediction market company Kalshi has hired a former FBI agent to run its first anti-money
laundering team.
NPR's Bobby Allen reports that prediction market firms are facing increased legal scrutiny
from state and federal regulators.
Former FBI agent and federal prosecutor Sean Fern will lead the team, their focus preventing
criminals in the U.S. and abroad from using Kalshi to launder money.
On a day-to-day basis, I think that involves knowing who our customers are, getting a better
understanding of where their money comes from, ensuring that we're not doing business with
sanctions entities or parties.
Prediction markets allow people to bet on sports, elections, politics, policy announcements.
They have exploded in growth, crossing $260 billion in bets this year.
That's triple last year's total.
But some of those bets have been the subject of investigations over insider trading and
market manipulation, like when former Congressman George Santos settled with regulators over
rigging a market.
Fern says part of his goal is to prevent the money laundering scandals that beset the cryptocurrency
industry.
Bobby Allen, NPR News.
A federal judge has ordered the White House to cancel any remaining taxpayer-funded television
ads promoting President Trump's political messages.
The Department of Homeland Security allocated $20 million for the campaign.
The judge issued a two-week restraining order Sunday night in a lawsuit challenging the spending.
The administration had argued the order was unnecessary because the ads were about to
stop airing.
The White House has defended the commercials as public service announcements.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel Prize in Economics for macroeconomic stabilization research
Trump says Russia and Ukraine agreed to energy ceasefire, but Zelensky says he knows nothing of it
North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles eastward into the sea, its fourth launch in a month
Tropical Storm Rachel pounds Long Beach and Southern California coast, damaging boardwalk and homes
Prediction market Kalshi hires former FBI agent Sean Fern to lead anti-money laundering team
Federal judge orders White House to cancel remaining taxpayer-funded Trump political TV ads
